hook: The patient warlord who unified Japan and began 250 years of peace.

pages.x: Ieyasu was born in 1543 in Okazaki Castle, the son of a minor lord in a Japan torn by civil war. At four he was sent as a hostage to a powerful clan, was kidnapped on the way by a rival, and spent most of his childhood as a hostage.

pages.t: Waiting for the bird to sing
pages.x: He allied with the warlord Oda Nobunaga, then served Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who unified Japan. A famous saying compares the three: if a bird will not sing, Nobunaga kills it, Hideyoshi makes it sing, and Ieyasu waits until it does.

In 1590 Hideyoshi gave him the Kanto plain in exchange for his old lands. Ieyasu made his base at a fishing village called Edo. By the 1700s it was one of the largest cities in the world. Today it is Tokyo.

After Hideyoshi died, Japan's lords split into two camps. On 21 October 1600, in fog at Sekigahara, about 160,000 samurai met. A rival general changed sides in the middle of the battle, and Ieyasu won.
In 1603 the emperor named him shogun, military ruler of Japan. He made the lords spend every other year in Edo and leave their families there as hostages, which kept them poor and loyal.
William Adams, an English navigator shipwrecked in Japan in 1600, became one of his advisers, built him Western-style ships and was made a samurai, the first Westerner to become one.
He died in 1616, aged 73, after a meal, a famous story says, of sea bream fried in a new style. He was worshipped as a god at a splendid shrine at Nikko.
Ieyasu ended a century of civil war and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, which gave Japan 250 years of peace, the Edo period, until 1868. His city of Edo became Tokyo.
pts: Began 250 years of peace in Japan
